The opinion reported in the Embassy's wire of May 31,
1943, no. 818 concerning current Japanese o1l production
in North Borneo and East Indies fields was confirmed by
the Netherlands Ambassador here who was interviewed by
Boehringer. The same opinion was also hald by the
Netherlands Military Attache who had just arrived from
London, -- namely that the Japanese were obtaining
approximately 10% of pre-war production or about 6,000,000
60,000,000.
barrels of oil instead of s0%.
The conviction that the Japanese would not be able to
carry through an intensive drilling program which would
result in the produotion rate approximating 60,000,000
barrels per annun in July this year is the basis for the
foregoing estimate. It was intimated by the Netherlands
Ambassador that Dutoh official:oiroles in London ourrently
held this same view.

Reference is made to the Embassy's telegram No.827,
June 2, 3 p.m., transmitting for the Board of Economic
Warfare summaries of economic reports taken from Japanese
radio broedcasts, obtained from Chinese and American
monitoring services in Chungking for the period May 10
to May 25, 1943, inclusive. There is herewith enclosed
more complete information on the material submitted as
894.50/203
well as reports not deemed important enough to be tele-
graphed.
The acting manager of the China Division, United
States Office of War Informetion, has informed the
Embassy that the Domei reports in English are monitored
Bac
by his organization as transmitted in Morse code. He
added that the Chinese service monitors Japanese reports
broadcast in Japanese kane. They are then translated
into Chinese and released in that language.
Respectfully yours,
1943
George Atcheson, jt.
Chargè d'Affaires a.i.

JAPAN PROPER
1. Discovery of Rich Vein of Zircon Reported.
Sendai, May 10.- The discovery of a rich vein
of zircon at the Manahata gold mine in Fukushima pre-
fecture will further bolster Japan's war time produotion
of eardinal metals since zircon is indispensable for the
production of special metals. It was said that during
experimental drilling at the gold mine it was found that
a high percentage of zircon could be obtained. Under the
Sendair mining inspection bureau, whioh will undertake an
extensive survey, mining experts from the Ministry of
Commerce and Industry will cooperate. (Domei in English).
2. Now Paint for Ship Bottom Use Said Invented.
Tokyo, May l0.- A professor of the Imperial
University of Kyoto has invented a new kind of paint for
the bottoms of vessels whioh does not oontain mereury.
It is remarked that, fartthe purpose of preventing
corrosion, the bottoms of vessels are usually painted
with ouprous oxide and merouric oxide. With regard to the
latter, however, Japan must depend on imports from abroad.
However, with the invention of the new paint we can do
without mereury. This will, of course, be very valuable
to shipbuilding. (Translated from Chinese).
3. Details of National Capital Mobilization and
Dafly Necessities Mobi11sation Plen for 1943-44
Tokyo, May 1l.- There were passed, at the

National Capital Mobilization Plan: Heretofore in
all capital control plans omphasis has been laid on the
accumulation and distribution of capital on the monetary
markets. Beginning with this fiscal year, however, the
seope of the plan is extended to cover the income of
the people and an allocation is made of the funds,
properties and people's requirements for consumption in
accordance with plans based on actual wartime economic
conditions of the people and the financial strength of
the country. This can then be called a truly nmational
capital plan. The basic principles used in the compila-
tion of the present plan follow:
(1) In the compilation of the 1943-44 National
Capital Mobilization Plan, the chief principle
is to push the economic aotivities necessary for
the prosecution of the war to the fullest extent,
taking into consideration the Materials and
esouroes Mobilization Plan, the Production
Expansion Plan, the National (Labor) Mobilization
Plan, and other plans.
(2) Another principle is to make an allocation of the
capital available for mobilization and amounts
of capital for the requirements of the people.
This capital will be taken from government re-
ceipts from taxes, funds mobilized from various
areas in Greater Éast Asia and the savings of
the people.
(3) The allocation of this capital for the expenditure
of the government and investment in industries or
in foreign countries shall take the war into first
consideration. The decision shall be made after
careful deliberation on the relative importance
of each category. Again, for the purpose of
coping with any changes in the situation, an
appropriate amount of capital funds shall be
reserved for making adjustments.
Daily Necessities Mobilization Plan: The present
fiseal year's plan is compiled for the purpose of ensuring
the people's livelihood which is for the proseeution of
the war and which is necessary. In view of the results
of the enforeemnt of the plan during the precedine fiseal
year end the conditions obtaining in the current fiseal
yeer, special consideration has been given to the following
points:
(1) Prineipal foodstuffs, household fuels, fiber
manufactures.- To mak the plans es eomprehensive

different eraraeteristios and the tendeney of
their supply am demand.

8. Mitsubishi Expands Its Wartime Industries.
Tokyo, May 25.- To cone with the increasing wartime
domands, the Mitsubishi Konzern, the control body of all

industries under its control. In this connection, Mitsubishi
has already approved the doubling of the capital of the
Mitsubishi Steel Manufacturing Company and the Mitsubishi
Chemieal and Industrial Company, its two giant subsidiaries.
It has also approved the establishment of a new Mitsubishi
Machine Tools Company. Other new activities of the Konzern
include: (1) the doubling of the Janan Building and Iron
Company to Yen 20,000,000: (2) expansion of the eapital of
the Japan Aluminum Works from Yen 6,900,000 to Yon 15,000,000;
(3) expansion of the canital of the Chosen Heavy Industries,
Limited, from Yen 7,000,000 to Yen 15,000,000; (4) the
establishment of Wooden Dockyards worth Yen 1,000,000 as
a substdiary of the Mitsubishi Warehousing Company, and
(6) expansion of the Mitsubishi O1l Company through the
creation of several new refineries. (Domei in English).

joint collaboration of eustoms officials concerned will be
realized when new customs regulations go into effect on
June 1, negotiations for which have been completed.
Eltminating unnecessary customs delays, the new regu-
lations call for the establishment of a bonded warehouse
in Tientsin and the dispatching of a Manchukuo custom
official to Tientsin to work in collaboration with the
Chinese custom officiels in jointlv inspecting goods
passing between the two countries via the overland route.
A greatly simplified customs procedure thus will be effected
at last, it is said. Freight cars, which formerly were
detained on the border on an average of seven days, now
will have to wait only half a day under the new transpor-
tation system. Lack of coordination between the customs
and the three countries necessitating repeated customs
inspection caused these long deleys heretofore. However,
undor the new regulations goods destined, for instance, for
Japan from North China will be shipped directly after
passing inspection of North China customs officials at
Tientsin. Goods going from Fusan to Tientsin will be
shipped henceforth directly to Tientsin, as bonded goods
upon passing Jananese customs inspection at Fusan. In
like manner, it is understood customs procedures for goods
passing over the border into Antung and Shanhaikwan will
be simplified considerably. (Domei in English).
Peiping, May 16.- With the development of the
Greater East Asia War, the land transportation of the
Japanese and Manchurian armies has grown in importance.
The cumbersome procedures required by the customs
authorities at Shanhaikwan of both the Chinese and
Manohurian governments in the past have much retarded the
expansion of transportation facilities. Hence, a set of
new measures has been decided upon whereby the accumulation
of goods at Shanhaikwan can be eliminated. The notifi-
cation promulgated by the Tientsin cus toms concerning this
matter reads as follows: "Effeotive from June 1, the
prosodures regarding the transportation of goods permitted
to be made from Shanhaikwan to Tientsin and vice versa
may be performed at the Tientsin customs ofrice". (Trans-
lated from Chinese).

16. Tunnel Under Yangtze Contemplated.
Tokyo, May 14.- The construction of a Yen
70,000,000 tunnel under the Yangtze River between Nanking
and Pukow is being contemplated by the Hwa-chung (Central
China) Railway Company, authoritative quarters here
revealed. The tunnel, which would connect the Tientsin-
Pukow railway and the Sha nghai-Nanking railway, would
make possible through railwav travel from Nanking to
Chosen as well as to Manchukuo via Tientsin and Peking.
At present, passengers and freight, which are increasing
rapidly, must be transported by ferry boats between
Pukow and Nanking, which are separated by about a one mile
expanse of the Yangtze. In the construction of the tunnel,
which is expected to take five years, the assistance of
the Japanese Railways Ministry, which recently successfully
constructed the Kwammon undersea tunnel between Moji and
Shimonoseki, will be sought and the latest boring methods
as well as machinery will be employed. The project, which
is now said to be in its initial stage, is expected to be
rushed to keep pace with the developments of the current
war. With the realization of the Shanghai-Singapore rail-
way, which is also being considered, the East Asiatic
Continental Railway from Singapore to Hailar, Manchukuo,
may be realized in the not too distant future, authorita-
tive quarters declared. (Domei in English).
Nanking, May 13.- With a view to eliminating the
necessity of crossing the Yangtze River from Nanking to
Pukow, it is planned to build a tunnel to conneet the
Shanghai-Nanking and Tientsin-Pukow railroads. The width
of the Yangtze here is about one mile. It is contomplated
to build the tunnel starting from Honingmen, about three

been decided to convert idle factories resulting from a
curtailment of the production of surplus agricultural

first sten, the idle sugar mills in Malang and Besoeki
provinces will be converted. Measures to provide for the
necessary personnel and equipment have already been taken.

this year. Having in th background Madoera Island, the
groatest salt producing cente in the East Indies, and an
ample labor markot, these caustic soda plants are assured
of a substantial output.
Paper and soap manufacturing will get the most
benefit from the increased production of caustic soda.

depended upon most of its supply from Japan and Soandinavia
in pre-war days, plans have al so been drawn to inorease
the produotion of paper. Besides the pulp produoed from

doeree not only aims to fill Japan's requirements by

ing the dema nd for lumber into urgent and non-urgent
categories, but also to furnish lumber at the lowest possi-

complete elimination of charges of the middlemen. Thus
the deoree may be said to embody the firm determination
of th Government Gensral of French Indoc ina to ceoperate
with Japan. (Domei in English).

attacked by the boll weevil and the Japanese authorities
were at a loss how to co pe with the situation due to the
laok of sprayers with which to spread the insecticides
which had arrived from Japan. However, the natives imme-

native bamboo. With the menace met, the cotton grew
rapidly and is now yielding a good harvest. (Domei in
English).

123. Develepment of West Borneo Reported.
Banjermasin, May 20.- The development of West
Borneo, whereof little has been reported owing to the
inconvenienee of the means of communications, is progress-
ing rapidly and satisfactorily, it was revealed today by
authorities of the naval administration who returned
today from an inspection tour of that region. Peace and
order in West Borneo is perfectly maintained. The
population of Pontienak and the vicinity rose to 63,000,
one-third of whieh is Chinese. Having lived here for
nearly three gemerations, the Chinese have almost forgotten
their own language. They are of a gentle disposition and
have sworn to cooperate wit h the na val administration.
Dyaks, who number some 200,000 of the total West Borneo
population of 1,O00,000, live in the interior. There is
probably no race on earth so lovable as the Dyak race.
Pure and innocent at heart, they deeply respect the
Jepanese who have freed them from 300 years of Dutch
oppression. Needless to say, the native inhabitants are
heartily cooperating with the Japanese aut horities whose
influenee is permeating to the interior with the establish-
ment of provincial administrative organs.
Having been spared almost entirely from the
ravages of the war, West Borneo has enjoyed remarkable
industrial development during one year and four months
since its occupation by the Jananese forces. It was noted
that from pre-war days the production of copra and crude
rubber in West Borneo has increased by leaps and bounds.
The output of copra has increased returns from which they
are now able to oover losses from crude rubber, resulting
in the curtailment of its production. Lumber production
is improving also. With the use of sea craft enoouraged,
lumber is now being exported to Java. Ironwood, mahogany,
and rattan exists in abundance. The output of mangrove
wherefrom tannin is attained now has reaohed a substantial
figure. Ocean routes to various parts of the. Co-Prosperity
Sphere have been establimhed and trade with North Borneo
is steadily increasing. Bus lines have been developed so
well that they are now considered to be the best in Borneo.
Badiating from Pontianak, the bus lines now extend over a
hundred kilometers to the interior amd are being actively
used by the native inhabitants. The education system is
being rapidly perfected, especially in the districts
centering around Pontianak, Besides elementary, secondary
and hisher public sehools, agricultural and normal sehools
have been opened. The Japanese language is being offered
as a regular eourse in all these schools. Night sohools
are else being eonducted for the benefit of sovernmental
effieials, and courses consisting of the Japanese language
and history are given. The zeal of the Chimese students
in the might soheels is so intense that classes are filled

and l0 per cent per annum and those on fixed deposits to
16.6 per eent.

puppet Philippine regime have independent financial systems.
The chier receipts of the Japanese military administration
have been the import and export duties and the prooeeds from
the tobaceo monopoly, while those of the puppet government
prior to the fall of Corregidor were confined to the taxes
oolleeted in Manila munieipality and its environs. The
puppots had to borrow money from the Japanese military
aaministration every month. However, owing to the expan-
sion of the tax jurisdietion, the initiation of new taxes
and the inerease in tax rates on wines, the puppet govern-
ment is now in a better conditions.
18. Gurrenay and Commodity Prices in P.I.

several times. This has given rise to drastie advanees in

of Taiwan, and other Japanese banks, the condition has
impreved slishsly. It has been decided that the rates of

JAPAN PROPER
1. Reports on Extraordinary Session of Diet.
Tokyo, May 2°/- The Government has decided to
convene an extraordinary session of the Diet for three
days beginning June 16 for the purpose of clarifying
measures to be taken by the Government towards fur ther
consolidating the national structure in successfully
prosecuting the war, which is in its decisive stage...
Matters pertaining to the further increased production
of war materials as well as adjustment of the domestic
economic structure are expected to be referred to in
the coming session of the Diet and preparations are
being made toward that end... (Domei in English).
Tokyo, May 28.- In the Cabinet meeting on
May 28 it was announced that the adjustment of industries
would be one of the problems on which discus sions would
be focussed in the coming session of the Diet. It is
said that the adjustment of industries this time will not
be confined to the rationalization of the organs for
prodution and distribution. On the contrary, it will
be extunded to cover the adjustment of all peace-time
industries and enterprises as well. Therefore all such
important categories as labor, capital, materials, power,
te., will be included. The measures contemplated are
designed to enable Japan to cope with the decisive stage
of the war...
The bills to be submitted to the Diet for discussion
include the following:
1. Budget Plans:
(a) Bill providing for increase in purohade
price of rice.
(b) Bill goverming emergency food produetion
plans.
(c) Bill providing for overhaul of plans for
various enterprises.

-2-
2. Legislative Bills:
(a) Public Loan Law bill which is related
to the budget plans.
(b) Special Account Law bill which is also
related to the budget plans.
(c)
Bill calling for revision of the National
Rehebilitation Treasury Law.
(d)
Bill of law governing edjustment of
utilization of capital for enterprise:.
(Broadcast in Japanese)
Details of Bill for Industrial Readjustment.
Tokyo, June 1.- The probl en on which discussions will
be directed in the forthcoming session of the Diet is
the readjustment of ind ustries. Some time ago plans were
formulated by the Planning Board, assisted by representa-
tives of such ministries as Army, Navy, Finance, Commerce
and Industry, Agriaulture and Forestry, and Tublic Welfare.
These plans were submitted to the regular Cabinet meeting
on June 1 and were formally aporoved. At 4 p.m. on June 1
the Board of Information mleased the outline and principles
of the industrial readjustment plans, which are designed
to strengthen the war potential, together with commen ts by
Director Gene ral Suzuki of the Planning Board. The funda-
mental principles for strengthening the war potential
and readjusting industries are as follow:
1. To concentrate all efforts on the five key
wartime industries (iron, coal, light metals,
airplanes and ships).
2. To direct those enterprises which ha ve not yet
been strengthened for war production to do so
as soon as possible.
3. To readjust and strengthen the important indus-
tries to a still greater extent.
Plans for induetrial readjustment are also provided
for in the bill of the law o verming capital for indus-
trial reedjustment, in the bill of the law go verning the
revision of the National Rehabilitation Treasury Law and
in budget plans.
The above bills will be submitted to the forthooming
session of the Diet for its deliberation, after whioh the
whole pieture of the readjustment plans will be given.
It is understood that they will be put into effect immedi-
ately after being approved by the Diet. (Broadcast in
Jepanese).
Tokyo, June 1.- The outline of the industrial read-
justment plans passed at the Cabinet meeting on June 1 is
given hereunder:
1. For the purpose of facilitating the prosesution
of the war and mmintaining the people's livelihood
during

-3-
during wartime by strengthening the war potent ial
directly to the highest degree, it is proposed
to extend the objectives of industrial readjust-

2. New Japanese-Style Truc Produced.

Technical Commission under the Ministry of Commerce

3. Clothing Material Made from Manila Hemp.
Kyoto, May 28.- A new proces& for manufacturing
clothing material out of Manila hemn, suitable for warm
elimate, has been perfected by Arisato Saito of the
Kyoto municipal textile experiment station. According to
Saito, Manila hemp is cut into bits of about one centi-
meter and treated with caustic soda. It is then mixed
with 20 percent of paper pulp which results in a paper
Fike material. This is then put through a specially
devfsed thread twisting machine. The thread thus produced
is similar in size to No. 16 thread of superior strength,
suitable for weaving purposes. Plans are now underway
to industrialize the new process and the first products
will be sent to soliders on the south Pacific fronts.
Seito is now experimenting on producing material suitable
for gauze and other medical purpose, by mixing his new
produet with staple fiber threads. (Domei in English).

6. Cork Oak Grown on Jananese Soil.
Osaka, June 1.- After eight long years of arduous
research, Yae Shirai, botanical exjert of the forestry
bureau of Osaka municipalitv, finaily succeeded in growing
cork oak (Quercus suber) on Jananese soil. It was in the
spring of 1938 that Shirai launched on the scientific
experiment to plant oak trees which existed in various
prefectures of the country and begen the difficult task
of raising the desired tree by grafting and other methods
at the forestry stations of Okayama and Tanabe. Simultane-
ously, similar experiments were carried out in other sections
of the country but without success. So difficult was the
projeet of discovering the proper method that Shirai even
thought of ending the experiment at one stage. However,
he continued with renewed vigor, gathering approximately
l0 species of oak as a basis of his endeavors. After
the study of climatic conditions, distribut ion of ferti-
lizer and effects of sunlight, they were able to grow
about 100 cork oak trees in the autumn of 1940. However,
they discovered that the plants would not thrive long.
Then one day a new experiment was started on a hint derived
from a supplementary experiment on femac (?) hormones.
Thereafter, close attention was given to proper nourishment
required by the plants, which assured complete success by
the autumn of 1941. It was learned that on receiving news
of this scientific victory, the Tokyo Linoleum and Nippon
beer companies have deeided to conduct large scale planting
of the new cork oak which will become the first cork oak
plantations in this country. Shirai told the interviewer:
"Now that various secrets to obtain the dirrieult eork
oak on Japanese soil have been solved, we are pleasantly
awaiting the day when wholesale planting of these trees
eah be mmde in the regions or Kechi aad Okayama prefeotures
as well as in Kyushu". (Domei in English).

34. Process to Conserve Vaccine Virus.
Fukuoka, May 29.- The Tokyo Army Surgeon School
has discovered a process to conserve vaccine virus for
one year or longer, another of a series of Japanese
medical triumphs since the outbreak of the war. Hitherto
vaccine virus could be preserved for only two months.
A plane of the Nipron Airways Cornoration, which arrived
here yesterday from Peking, unloaded a small tin container
containing valuable lymph vaccine cultured from calf
intestines. Surgeon Nitsugi Tanaka, Tokyo Arny School
surgeon, who arrived here to receive the tin, explained
that after assiduous research, his school succeeded in
discovering a method of preserving vaccine virus for
a year or longer. He added that the Army Surgeon School
is intending to add finishing touches to the new dis-
covery by experimenting with vaccinevirus which was sent
from Peking. He asserted that with the new method it
will be easier to eradicate smallpox throughout the Go-
Prosperity Sphere.

55. Two New Methods of Making Paper Invented.
Tokyo, June 15.- Paper is one of the important
materials in wartime. It is therefore imperative to
increase its production and at the same time to curtail
its consumption. Recently two valuable inventions
concerxing paper have been suocessfully completed by
two Japanese simultaneously. The first Japanese is Ohta
of the fiber chemistry section of the Kyoto Imperial
University. Usually the timber produced in the southern
regions is regarded as unsuitable for manufacturing white
paper due to the fact that it is of many kinds and not
uniform in hardness which makes it impossible to treat
it chemically with the existing sulfurio acid process.
Moreover, bleaching is difrfoult. Ohta, however, has
imvented a new process by using bisulfurio acid (?) to
overcome these difficulties following his researches of
the fibers of timber produced in the Philippines, Borneo
and other sout hern areas. It has been decided to put
his process into industrial use. The other Japanese
1s Nakamura of Kyoto who invented a kind of solution
ioh when applied to paper makes it several times as
A dprable as oraimmry thior paper. (Broadeast

=== Page 124 === (confidence 0.98)
-25-
Kyoto, June 15.- The Japanese-occupied southern
regions will become an outstanding world source of paper
pulp if the experimental manufacture of pulp from southern
timber now being conducted by Nagakatsu Ohte of the Kyoto
Imperial University proves successful. Ohta is an exnert
attached to the fibrous chemistry section of Kyoto
Imperial Universit y and has made exclusive study of the
special chemical process for manufacturing pulp from
Philippine and Borneo timbers whicl pulp me kers in the
past had given up as completely unfit for pulp manufac-
ture. To overcome the difficulties of pulp manufacture
by using sulfuric acid, Ohta devised a new process
employing sulfurous acid. Under the new process, the
irregular qualities of the southern timbers were conquered
and the manufacture of white paper from southern timbers
hitherto regarded as impossible was made possible without
great difficulty. The new process is expected to be
Industrialized in the near future. (Domei in English).

Shanghai, June 2.- Economic relations betwoan
North and Central China have become increasingly close
of late, and exchange of commodities between the two
regions is rapidly increasing, stated Viscount Viichi
Sakatani, adviser to the Central Reserve Bank of China,
who returned here today after a brief tour of inspection
of economic conditions in Central Chine. He continued,
"In my opinion, the rigid barter system now in practice
will be displaced by more flexible system of exchange
in which case North China may witness an excess of
imports over exports, while settlements of accounts may
be made under the system similar to that in practice
botween North China and Manchukuo. It is to be hoped",
he added, "that some suitable system that will place
equal emphasis on commodities as well as value transac-'
tions will be devised in place of the present system which
omphasizes value only. Central Reserve Bank notes have
become very stable and to further strengthen the ir
position various kinds of savings banks and institutions
have been emphasizing greater savings with marked suecess",
he stressed. He pointed out that it is the policy of the
bank to develop spinning and light industries with increas-
ing production of daily necessities. "Rela tions between
various banks in China and the Central Reserve Bank are
being earried out smoothly, but we would like to strengthen
this factor", he said. Deposits are now in ercees of
Yon 160,000,000. Regarding exchange probhhms between
North and Central China, he said, "I cannot say anything
definite, however, I believe that a satisfactory measure
must be enforced to safeguard the smooth flow of commo-
dities and prevent abnormal rise of commodity priees".

84. Activities of Central Reserve Bank Restricted.
Shanghai, June 3.- The National Goveinment of
China (Nanking regime) is planningto streamline the

exelusive control organ. Under the new plan, the
Central Reserve Bank is expected to confine loaning
funds to monetary organs dispensing with the practice
of extending private loans to merchants so as to func-

also to direct efforts towards concentrating to the

the bank's structure as the central bank of Central
China. (Domei in English).

to one of assuring the people of Malaya of their essential

by the authorities of the Japanese military administration.

of Negri Sembilan will thus solve the outstanding economic

inerease the production of rice, potatoes, tapioca and oorn.

168. Conditions in North Borneo Reported.
By a Domei correspondent in Kuching, June ll.-
During my reoent inspection trip of North Borneo, I
witnessed everywhere through the entire area including
Banguey Island, scenes of activity both in agricultural
and fishing induatries. The fishing industry thrives at
Banguey Island, located off the tip of North Borneo, and
approximately io hours by vessel from Sandakan, capital
of North Borneo. Here I found ll4 Japanese fishermen
engaged in the fish canning industry. Before the outbreak
of the Greater East Asia Wer, Banguey Island canned tuna
was exported to many countries incl ding the United States.
Even before the outhreak of the war Banguey was known as
"Nippon Island" for the reasons that the Rising Sun flag
was seen fluttering on the island throughout the year
and our laboring hends are responsible for the island's
development. The Borneo Aquatic Products Company leased
Banguey Island from Britain in 1938 and immediately
established canning factories on the island. From January,
1939, the company began manufacturing canned fish and
dried bonito, annually producing 50,oo0 cases of canned
fish before the current war.
Kudat harbor area situated in the northern part
of the east coast, the residenoy of the former British
Borneo Governor, which I also visited, is mainly an
agrioultural district. Kudat is noted as the collecting
and distributing center for rubber, copra, corn and other
egrioulturel products and is also famed for its prosperous
livestock breeding industry. Eggs are also abundant and
before the outbreak of the current war, Kudat annually
exported 50,000 cases to Singapore. Kudat's population
numbers 31.000 of whioh 17,000 are native inhab1tants and
6.O00 Chinese. The entire population of Kudat is thamkful
over the releese frcm British oppression and is happily
working under Japenese administration. As en example of
their zenewed industry, they have inoreased the So0 eeres
of local paddy fieles under cultivation before the war
to 1,400 aeren, (Damei 1n mglish).

174. Report on Conditions in Thailand.
Bangkok, June 5.- Since its declaration of war
against the United Kingdom and the United States of America
on January 25, l942, Thailand, being one of the important
members of the Greater Rast Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere,
has dedioated all 1ts resources to the cause or the Greater
Bast Asia War. No efforts have been spared to establish
a wartime economio structure whereby the free economic
polioy has been converted into a controlled polioy. Daily
neoessities have been strictly economized and production
has been expanded. Such plans were launched from the
beginning of l942 and by now they have approached a stage
of actual enfereement. With regard to the restriotion of
profiteering, severe measures have been adopted. striking
developments have also been achieved in the strengthening
of control over important industries and the promotion
of light industries. Special efforts have been exerted
towerd the restrietion of profiteering, Sinee its

On Apri1 30, 1943, 1t was promulgated by the supreme
headquarters of Thailand's army for national defense
that hoarding of medical supplies and other important
materials or profiteering should be liable to death
punishment.
With regard to important industries, control
measures have been enforced successively. In February,
l943, the Thai Government promulgated a set of regulations
governing the control over cotton, made effective as from
April. According to these regulations, no cotton shall
be sold or moved without governmental permission. The
maximum prices for cotton piece goods have also been fixed.
Present stocks of cotton textiles in Thailand are consider-
able in quantity. This step is intended to maintain a
smooth supply. With regard to paper, a set of measures
for controlling the paper industry was promulgated in
the official gazette on February 20. All factories
manufacturing paper have been placed under governmental
management for the purpose of remedying the paper shortage
and to promote production. A system for the distribution
of paper has also been instituted with the object of
satisfying the requirements of important circles and
controlling the export and import of this commodity.
Official prices have also been fixed.
On April 29, 1943, an ordinance was promulgated
authorizing control over motor vehicles. Permission
must be obtained before any such vehicle can be registered,
sold, transferred or leased.
With regard to agriculture, steps have been
taken ever since the outbreak of the Greater East Asia
War to effect improvement. Thailand is originally an
agricultural nation. Since the war, it has also taken
the responsibility of supplying foodstuffs to areas
within the Co-Prosperity Sphere. It is but natural that
it should have done so. The recent agricultural policies
of Thailand may be described under the following two
headings: (1) Steps taken to maintain the supply of food-
sturfs and other farm produots, and (2) efforts made to
inerease the production of cotton and other important
agricultural produets.

light industries, which also forms one of the important
items of Thailand's wartime economic policy. This
includes the expansion of the production of daily
necessities. With regard to cotton textiles, not only
control has been enforced but steps have also been taken
to attain self-sufficiency. Some time ago a spinning

BI-MONTHLY APPRAISAL OF JAPAN'S

=== Page 173 === (confidence 0.99)
Summary*
Previous trends in the procurement of war materials
have continued. An effort to expand cottonproduction is
being pushed in suitable areas throughout the East Asia
sphere. The campaign is still in the experimental stage,
however, with many serious obstacles yet to be overcome.
Similar attempts are being made to solve the problems in-
volved in the production and distribution of food in East
Asia. Increased capital investments in Manchuria are con-
centrated on the expansion of coal, iron, and steel.
Japan's output of ships, both steel and wooden, has
begun to increase. Together with various measures of econ-
omy, this output will enable Japan to end the year with a
shipping position not materially worse than now exists.
Although the position is tight, it is not serious enough to
paralyze Japan's war effort unless the current rate of
attrition increases.
The aftermath of the Diet crisis last winter is
evident in Tojo's appointment of business advisers to the
Cabinet and in Ministerial shifts favoring the Diet leaders
and the old-line Foreign Office circles. These concessions,
while still leaving final powers in Tojo's hands, will tend
to close the rifts that had developed in Japan's ruling groups
and establish greater unity in prosecution of the war.
Japanese policy in China has been increasingly marked
by close coordination of political, economic, and military
operations, designed to strengthen the Nanking regime and
"soften up" the National Government in Chungking.

of Japan's position contained in EP-60, this issue of the
Bi-Monthly Appraisal has been altered to include a cross-
section of some of the more recent analyses of Japanese
war potential.

I. FUNCTIONAL DEVELOPMENTS
Significant developments of an overall functional
character have occurred in the fields of raw materials,
transportation, and administration.
Raw Materials
Recent reports from radio broadcasts and other sources
on Japan's activities in East Asia reveal that the Japanese
are making strong efforts to offset shortages of several
commodities through adjustments in their agricultural pro-
grams. A shortage of lubricating oil has stimulated efforts
to increase the production of castor beans in all parts of
East Asia where the crop will grow, and has also produced
attempts to manufacture lubricants from palm oil, cocoanut
oil, and rubber. A shortege of chemical fertilizers, which
probably cannot be overcome to any great extent, has brought
about attempts to increase the use of organic materials and
to develop the fertilizer resources of occupied territories.
A need for more horses for military use has inspired cam-
paigns to increase horse breeding and to improve the dis-
tribution of horse feed in Japan and Manchuria. A shortage
of protein food fram animal sources has led to special
efforts to increase the supply of meat and fish. In some
of the occupied territories, price control measures have
been instituted in an effort to bring down the high prices
of meat.
Activities in Cotton Expansion Program. Of all
shortages in East Asia, that of cotton may prove most
embarrassing to the Japanese, because it deprives them of
material which they would otherwise use as a means of ob-
taining supplies from all the occupied regions. An active
campaign is being pushed to increase cotton production, but
many serious obstacles have yet to be overcome.
Evidence of the shortage of cotton in East Asia con-
tinues to accumulate. Various methods of approach to the
problem &re being pursued. Further restrictions on the use
of cotton in clothing materials for the Japanese consumer
have been enforced. More spinning mills in Japan.are closing
down, indicating that little or no cotton cloth: will be manu-
factured in Japan for export. At the same time, machine
equipment for textile mills is being transferred to:other
areas, including Manchuria, Thailand, Burma, and the Philip-
pines. Effort is mainly concentrated, however, on expand-
ing the production of raw cotton.

Areas in which efforts aro being made to introduce
or expand cotton production include North China, the
Philippine Islands, tho Netherlands East Indies, Burma,
Thailand, and Malaya. Only in the first of these has
any significant amount of cotton been.previously grown:
In North China, moreover, the type of cotton produced is
not satisfactory and the Japanese are reported to be es-
tablishing special plantations for the purpose of obtain-
ing seeds of superior quality. The five southern torri-
torios montioned havo all been large importers of cotton
goods in the past. Plantings of cotton in these torri-

offer obstacles to success in North China and the Philip-

it would seom that Japan's ambitious cotton program is still
in the stage of planning, promotion, and experimentation.
Efforts to Reduce Foodstuffs Shortage. Genoral: food
shortages. are felt to various degrees in much of the East
Asia sphere. To supply these deficits, considerable effort
is being exponded to wring the last possible ton of food
out of certain of the occupied areas. Programs intended
to increase food production are under way throughout East
Asia, and upon their success hinge other programs to ex-
tract fibers and other industrial crops.
Japan is engaged in many a ctivities, based on both
short-and long-term plans, for solving problems concerning
the production and distribution of food in the East Asiatic
sphero. The principal deficit areas at the present time
appear to be Japan Proper, Occupied North China, Occupied
South China, the Philippines, Thailand, Malaya, and the
rubber producing districts and other Iocal areas in the
Netherlands East'Indies. On the othor hand, major sources
of food supply are Manchuria, Occupied Central China,
Formosa, French Indo-China, and Burma. Koroa which would
ordinarily be a source of surplus food supply, will be of
little help until the autumm of 1943 becauso of the short
crop of rice in 1942.
Strenuous offorts aro being made to increase food
production in Japan Proper; in spite of shortages of
fertilizers, spray materials, and farm labor. These ef-
forts are not likely to be vory successful. An equally
intensive campaign is boing waged to squeeze a greater net
agrioultural dividend from Manchuria, both by swelling the

and by decreasing the demands of Manchurian urban markets.

Drastic:efforts are. being exerted to obtain the last portions
of the 1942: food crops from Central China, even in the face
of starvation conditions prevailing in the large Central
China cities. Large amounts of rice and corn have been
roquisitioned from Indo-China, and accumulated supplies of
rice in Burma are being tapped. In the Philippines,
Thailand, Malaya, and various parts of the Netherlands
East Indies, programs to increase the production of food
to meet the needs of Japanese forces and the local popu-

Evidence of a deficiency of fish and meat in Japan
Proper and several of the occupied countries has begun to
appear. The Japanese are trying to offset what is appar-
ontly a severe shortage of hogs in Japan by such unusual
means as catching seals for meat as well as fur and trying
to persuade miners to raise hogs, goats, and rabbits.
Shortages of meat are indicated in Thailand and the Philip-
pines. The Japanese have established very strict control
over the fishing industry of the Philippines, and are ex-
ploiting that of Burma for the benefit of their armed forces.
They are actively planning to increase the fish production
of the East China Sea and are making strong efforts to
develop all fishing possibilities in the southern regions.
The construction of frozen fish plants on Celebes is one
feature of the program to exploit these resources.
Japan's efforts to increase the production and con-
trol the distribution of food in East Asia are designed
primarily to further the prosecution of the war without
regard to the well being of the local inhabitants. The
most favorable outcomes of these efforts probably will not
prevent malnutrition and outright starvation from occurring
in Occupied North China, in the cities of Central China,
in Occupied South China, in Thailand, in Malaya, and in parts
of the Netherlands Indies. On the other hand, working groups
engaged in the production of strategic commodities will un-
doubtedly receive preferential treatment. The short food
supply in the Philippines will hinder programs for the
production of industrial agricultural products. The food
supply of Japan itself would be most seriously crippled
by the loss of Manchuria, Formosa, or Indo China.
Administration
Little detailed information on Premier Tojo's use of
the ordinance powers approved by the Diet has been fortooming.
Direct government supervision of the five designated key war
industries--iron and steel, coal, shipbuilding, airplanes,

and light metals--is evidently being effected. The new
ordinance powers facilitate a rationalized utilization
of raw materials, labor power, machine tools, and other
factors in order to stimulate expansion of output by
these industries. Application of the new ordinance
powers to other industries, however, has apparently been
delayed. There is some evidence that the operators not

The strong opposition which Tojo encountered in the
Diet session has led to a number of significant adjust-
ments within Japan's ruling groups. On the whole, these
adjustments indicate a modification of Tojo's previous
offorts to concentrate exclusive powers in his own hands,
disregarding the business interests, the Diet, and the
Foreign Office. In his recent moves Tojo has sought to
appease each of these groups.
Formation of Cabinet Advisers Council. On March 17,
1943, coincident with Tojo's announcement that the ordinance
powers had received Imperial approval, a set of new advisory
and executive organs was attached to the Cabinet. Seven
leading industrialists and financiers were constituted as
a Cabinet Advisers Council; together with the Cabinet,
they constituted a Wartime Economic Council. Through this
latter organ, the business interests were enabled to in-
fluence directly the administration of the wartime econ-
omy; in particular, they were enabled to curb the arbitrary
exercise of Tojo's new ordinance powers. The texts of the
documents establishing the advisory organs effectively re-
tained final powers in Tojo's hands, but the high rank
bestowed on the new advisers (equivalent to the status of
Cabinet Ministers) and the importance of their position in
Japan's business world made it certain that their advice
would not be lightly disregarded. The working partnership
between the Army and Big Business thus became an officially
ostablished fact in the highest level of administration.
The Reconstruction of the Cabinet. This move, ef-
fected one month later tham the formation of the Cabinet
Advisors Council, was largely designed to appease the Diet
leaders and disgruntled Foreign Office ciroles.. Both the
Minseito and Seiyukai parties, though now dissolved, are

Occupied China: Trends in Japanese Policy
Japan's policy in China in recent months has been
marked by close coordination of economic, political, and
military operations. A comprehensive campaign of formal
concessions in the political field has been accompanied
by readjustments in economic policy. At the same time, an
intensification of military action and a tightening of the
blockade against Free China have been initiated.
Political Concessions. The political campaign, which
began with Nanking's declaration of war against Britain and
the United States in January 1943, has been designed to build
up the prestige of that government as the National Government
of China. Cons iderable publicity has been given to the retro-
cession of special rights and to the restoration of Chinese
sovereignty through the relinquishment of extraterritoriality,
but these concessions have been made primarily for their
propaganda effect, and do not represent a real yiclding of
political authority. The Nanking regime still operates under
the Groctor East Asia Ministry and the Japanese Ambassador.
C
On March 30th, Japan formally returned to the Nanking
government the Concessions which it held in eight Chinese cities
(Hangohow, Soochow, Tientsin, Hankow, Shasi, Amoy, Foochom,
and Chungking). On the same day, there vas a ceremony for the
restoration to China of the administrative rights of the Lega-
tion Quarter in Peiping. This cession of rights was made vith
certain reservations, however, ponding the sottlement of the
terms of retrooession in the extraterritorial negotiations,
conferences on vhich mere scheduled to begin in May.

has reservod tho oxtratorritorial rights enjoyod by the Italian

In the various ceremonies and agreements that have

National Government of China, and the retrocession of rights
has been to that government. Great Britain and the United
States relinquished their extraterritorial rights (October
1942) to the Chungking government; Japan and the European Axis
powers have returned their concessions to Nanking. These
privileges were originally yielded by the Chinese government;
they had therefore to be returned to a national government of
China. Thus, it was necessary as well as expedient to re-
present Nanking as the National Government of China, although,
in reality, Japan's policy of maintaining separate political
entities in North China and Inner Mongolia has not been altered.
As part of the campaign to represent Nanking as the
government of China, Japan has also formally transferred
(March 29th) to that government the enemy assets seized by
Japanese armed forces in China. These properties number more
than a thousand and are primarily British and American. It
has never been made clear whether these properties are to be
held in custody or have been confiscated outright.
The politioal build-up has been designed not only to
establish Nanking, along with "Manchoukuo", as a member of
the family of nations, but also to remove from the puppet
officials the stigma of traitors and to encourage other Chinese
leaders to take part in the government. In this endeavor there
has becn some sucdess. Early in March, Tokyo announced that
five prominent financial and political leaders, formerly
connected with the Chungking government, had agreed to cooperate
with Nanking and that three of the five had become members of
the National Economic Council.
For both political appeasement and for economic reasons,
Japanese polioy is now directed toward withdrawal of their
own military from active administration of the Occupied China
aroa, and greater participation by the Nanking puppet govern-
ment is indicated. The suspension of the issue of military
yen, the abolition of military permits for most commodities in
tho local trade, and the implementation of civilian trade con-
trol organizations are some of the recent developments that
give greater administrative authority to the puppet government.
This government is still controlled and directed by Japanese
advisors and officials, but some of the machinery has shifted
from military to civilian auspicos.
Economic Adjustment. More significant than these changes
is the recent adjustment of Japan's economic policy in China.
In arder to achieve greator production and more complete exploi-
tation, a new economio policy of appeasement has been adopted.

Overscas Chinese in the Southwest Pacific
Therc are about 2, 300, O00 Overseas Chinosc in British
Malaya, 1,600,000 in the Netherlands East Indies, and
118,000,000 in the Philippines--a total of over 4,000,000,
which constitutes by far the largest alien group in the
Southwest Pacific. In each of these three countries the
Chinese, with their long-established domination in commerce,
form an integral and principal part of the economic structure.
Malaya. The Malayan Chinese, forming 43 percent of the
population, are even more numerous then the natives. Under
the Japanese occupation. there are indications of unrest and
unemployment, although the Japanese Military Administration
has enlisted a large number of the destitute Chinese to repair
and improve highvays, harbors, and naval installations, and
to build various types of ships to facilitate communications
in the Southern Regions.
In 1937, Chinese invostments were said to have totaled
well over U.S. $200 million, ranking second only to those of
the British. Chinese owned 31 percent and operated at least
11 percent of the tin mines. Their holdings in rubber were
about 16 percent. They dominated almost all the retail trade
and controlled the pineapple industry, saw mills, factories
manufacturing various kinds of consumption goods, vegetable
farming, and livestock breeding. The present loss of world
markets and the consequent drop in the prices of rubber and tin
to an unbelievably low level are an index to the disastrous
effect the existing economic maladjustment has on Chinese
entrepreneurs.
Inasmuch as the Malayan Chinese have established
themselves as financiers, plantation owmers, traders, and
proceosors of agricultural and mineral commodities, the Japanese
Administration is using them as intermediaries between producers
and Japanese interests. Japanese intimidating and placating
methods of obtaining Chinese cooperation consist of (1)
threat of reprisal against the person involved or relatives
in China; (2) propaganda through the press and schools; (3)
recognition of Chinese right- to cultivate rice; and (4)
permission for the Chinmse to make small menthly remittances
to faril:es in occupied China.
Netherlands Esst Indies. In their economic position,
the Chinege in the Netherlands East Indies are as important
as those in British Malaya, although in the Netherlands Ecst
Indies they constitute only a little pter 2 percent of the
Dutoh East Indiam.population and ennounter a more severe

=== Page 189 === (confidence 0.99)
-15-
co petition from the Indonesians. Their importance is
illustrated by the fact that they had been receiving 20 per-
cent of the country's total income. Their investments, ranking
second only to those of the Dutch, ere estimated at about
U.S. $150 million or 1l percent of all private capital in the
area. In the production of raw materials, in industry, and
in transportation there vere around 320,000 skilled and
unskilled Chinese laborers. Of the entire Chinese working
population, 52 percent were workmen of this type and 38 percent
vere ongaged in large and small trados.
Because the Chinose in thc Netherlands East Indies not
only occupied the position of middlemen, but were also employed
in the production of foodstuffs, raw materials, and consumers
goods, and because these are the very places where the Japanese
now want them to be, the booupational maladjustment that these
Chinose have enoountered is not half as scrious as that
encountered by the Chinese in Malaya.
Tho Philippine Islands. In the Philippincs the Chinese
were prominent in the warehous ing, marketing, shoemaking,
and the cordage buiness, They controlled over 10 percent
of the capital invested in the lumber industry, and their
influence in banking was not negligible.
The Japanesc Military Administration has cstablished a
Bureau of Commerce and Indus try to break the Chinese control
of retail trade in favor of Filipino nationals. A system
of insuring permanent Filipino control of domestic trade
is said to have been established.
Conclusion. In the Southwest Pacific, tho Overseas
Chinese are generally regarded as militantly patriotic. This
mas demonstrated by their boycott of Japanese goods and by
their large monotary contributions to Chungking. During the
course of the Japanese invasion, several thousand young
Overseas Chinose volunteered to enter the Chinese army. It was
undoubtedly for these reasons that the Japanese later took
reprisals, resulting in the execution and imprisonment of many
Chinese.
Because of their past affiliations with Chungking, their
appreciation of the advantages under former governments, and
their deep distrust of Japanese intontionm, the Overseas Chinese
in the Southwest Pacific are anti-Japanese and non-cooperative
in spirit. They are not likely to change their attitude
as long as they have confidence in China's final victory and in
the ability of the United Nations to reoccupy their countries.
In fact, arti-Japen activities etill persist in Malaya.

ontirely ignored, if not sacrificed, the interests of the

In the Netherlands East Indies, the Japanese appear to have

Japan's Supply of Machinery for Occupied Areas
The Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce has recently
completed a study of the normal imports of important materials
by the presently occupied territory from non-occupied areas.
One conclusion to be irawn from this study is that Japan may
experience considerable difficulty in maintaining the effi-
ciency of machinery operation desired in industry and public
utilities over the East Asia sphere as a whole.
A review of the trade of the occupied areas over a
period of several consecutive years, usually including 1934
to 1939, shows that the average value imports of machinery
and tools of each area from European or American sources
amounted to the following percontages of the total machine
trade:
Philipoine Islands 97%

The 64 percent figure for China may be excessive as it is
known that some Japanese merchandise meved into China subsequent
to 1937 without clearance through the Customs. The 23 percent
figure for Manchuria does not reflect the true conditions for
some of the machinery credited to Japan actually originated
elsewhere. Eliminating these two markcts, the average for
all other areas is 94 percent.
From the southern areas Japan must secure minerals, in-
cluding petroleum products, tin, lead, zinc, iron, copper,
chromite, and bauxite; agricultural products including rice,
corn, and sugar; and such miscellaneous items as lumber and
cordage fibres. Japan's current needs will not require the
same amount of machinery previously utilized in these areas,
but it may be desirable to operate some industries at full
capacity in order to move stocks of materials and processed
goods to Japan. In addition, much is required in the way of
power machinery to servico public utilities which are so
necessary in all urban centers and for communications and
transport facilities.
Some of the equipment in these areas has been destroyed
or badly damaged, and some is in need of replecement parts
and repairs. Great Britain, Sweden, Germany, France, and möre
rocontly Switzerland have not been in a position to supply new

machinery, or, in many cases, even parts since 1939. It is
reasonable to belicvo that some of the equipment which was
operating in 1939 is no longer serviceable or is rapidly
becominginofficient.
It is probable that a Japaneso machine sorving the
same general purpose will not roadily fit into a series of
machines of French or British manufacture. The adjustments
may require so much in labor, time, and special materials
not readily available that it will be physically impossible
to sorvice the many various types of machines. Adequate
transport, -- rail, boat, and motor -- domands a great deal
of machinory. Thousands of motors are required and while
Japan has a good electrical industry, thore is some question
as to whother Japan is prepared to supply and maintain all
of tho clectric power equipment needed.
The machinery must be maintained by replacements or
accessories from Japan if that country is to benefit from
procossing near sources of supply, thereby easing the Iabor
problem and minimizing shipping difficulties. This will not
only ontail special jobs o dic-casting, tooling for many
varied designs of machines, and a high percontago of skilled
manpower hours, but thoro will also be delays awaiting pro-
duction and transport. Offsotting this in part, is the
probable presont surplus equipment proviously used in sugar
centrals, various mining venturcs, and possibly motors which
can bo adaptod to other uses.
Theso obstaclos may bo overcome by re-equipping vital
industrios and utilitios with Japanoso manufactures which aro
the result of mass production, and for which interchangeable
parts are readily available, or by moving all raw materials,
the securing of which demands the minimum in machinery, to
Japan for processing. The first alternative may prove more
beneficial if there is time to make the changes and if Japan
has the surplus machinery. If materials are brought to
Japan together with the existing equipment, the servicing
of the machinery is facilitated, but shipping and labor prob-
lems are accentuated. There is an irreducible minimum re-
quired for petroleum refining, mineral mining and processing,
transport, nd steam, gas and electric powered engines.
Unless Japanese capacity is greater than is now be-
lieved, it may be impossible for Japan to secure the maxi-
mum benefit of materials available in the southern regions
because of inability to supply the required machinery.

Burma and Railway Transport in Southeast Asia.
Continuous bombing attacks on the rail lines of
Burma have seriously hampered Japanese efforts to maintain
an efficient system of rail transport.
The four countries of Southeast Asia, Burma, Thailand,
and Indo-China, and Malaya--have meter gauge railroad systems
which would make it eventually possible for all rolling stock
to be interchanged. The Thailand-Malaya lines actunlly
form one continuous system vithout a break. The Indo-China
and Thailand systems, which were previously separated by a gap
between Phnom Penh and Saigon, have apparently been linked by
a light line with a ferry at the Mekhong River. The Burma
and Thailand systems are being connected by a line from
Kanchanaburi in Thailand to Ye at the extreme s outhern end
of the Burma railways. The eagerness of the Japanese to link
these railways indicates how important it is to them to have
a united system. Once the links are in operation, any lack
of engines or rolling stock in one section can be satisfied
quickly by moving material from a less aotive sector.
Thus far the Malaya, Thailand, and Indo-China systems
are evidently operating as complete units, and have suffered
slight damage. The Thailand line is eapecially necessary for
the transportation of goods to the northern army from the port
at Bangkok. The Burma system has borne the brunt of attack.
Severel months ago the destruction of bridges had already
caused it to fall into five segments as follows:

Tojo's Remarks on Domestic Economic Problems.
Tokyo, June 16.- (Extracted from Tojo's speech
to the Diet on June 16). "Fortunately our industrial
production has been remarkably improved and expanded
since the latter part of lest year. The Covernment will
further reinforce the war structure with the wholesale
cooperation of the people and concentrate all the efforts
of the nation on the augmentation of the fighting power.
It is for this purpore that the Government petitioned the
throne to convoke the present extraordinary session of
the Diet and submitted the budget and bills relating to
the adjustment of enterprises and an emergency increase
in the production of food. The proposed readjustment in
enterprises is intended to make the entire nation contri-
bute to the augmentation of the fighting power by extend-
ing the principle of past readjustment of enterprises and
execute a thorough-going readjustment in every department
of industry. The concerted effort of the entire nation
is absolutely necessary for the smooth execution of this
plan. All the people are urged, therefore, to appreciate
the Government's intentions and cooperate with the Govern-
ment positively by completing the readjustments as soon as
possible by placing the right man in the right place so as
to enable each to give full play to his abilities.
"The measure under contemplation will entail defray-
ment of several milliard yen. The bill for disposing of
the fund for readjustment of enterprises hes been speoially

=== Page 200 === (confidence 0.99)
-2-
fund to be defrayed. The entire Japanese people, who
already have been endeavoring to increase savings and
economize on consumption, are requested to redouble
their efforts, to check the floating purchasing power
and to preserve the netional economic order. It is
hardly necessary to mention that the Government is taking
all possible measures with regerd to food which is neces-
sary for the safeguarding of the netionel livelihood
during wartime. At the present stage of the war, however,
particularly strenuous efforts must be put forth for
attaining self-support and self-sufficiency in food by
paying consideration to all contingencies. In line with
this policy the Government intends to effect an epochal
increase in the production of rice, barley, wheet,
potatoes and other foodstuffs with a view to placing the
matter of food supnlies in 8 most reassuring position in
these critical times.
"While conducting the administration in a most
efficient manner, the Government intends to merch forward
toward final victory by suspending or abandoning all
activities having no direct bearins unon the prosecution
of the war and mobilize both the Government and the
peonle for war production. It is in line with this
policy that the Government decided not to hold elections
for the prefectural assemblies this vear and submitted
the legislation bill relating to it. It is my earnest
desire that you gentlenen, understandin the Government's
intentions which I have just stated, will deliberate over
and speedily apnrove the budget and legislation bills
submitted by the Government." (Domei in English).

Statement on Industrial Readjust ent Issued by
President of Industrial Dedication Association.
Tokyo, June 18.- In order to achieve victory it is
essential to carry out industrial edjustments. The same
question has also been put forth in the meeting of the
Decisive War Conference. The deterrination of producers
in the rear is further strengthened. Every national
declares his willingness to sacrifice everything for
the nation. According to the published statement made
by the president of the Industrial Dedication Association,
the industrial adjustme nts this time aim at promoting
productive capacity to the maximum dur ing the period of
decisive war. All the industries, labor and manpower not
urgently required will be diverted to important industries.
Both in motive and in nature, these are entirely different
from the industrial adjustments of the past when depression
prevailed. In time of depression adjustments were rendered
necessary because of the surplus of manpower and materials.
The present indus trial adjustments, however, are directed
tawards mobilizing all the forces of the nation in order
to increase fighting strength. After the change of
profession is effected, the diverted manpower and materials
will manifest new strength. Although the peonle who are
leaving their old posts are fraught with grief, the
Government will make the best disposition of the matter
and take steps to ensure their livelihood. (Domei in
Japanese).

3. New Electrolytic Smelting Process for Copper,
Zinc and Lead.
Tokyo, June 1a.- A revoluti nery electrolytic
smelting process for conner, zinc and lead, displacing old
methods, has passed the test with flying colors in the
Tokyo Imperial Universi ty recently. Iresent were the
foremost experts of the universit, Jrnerial Technological
Institute, the Commerce and Industry Ministry and Mining
Control Association. The inventor, Takeo Kogawa, is a
technician of the Nippon Kogyo Company. The new smelt-
ing process requires simply a small amount of electrioity
and a simple electroliser. It does away with the neces-
sity of blast furnaces, coal cokes and other materials
such as silicates and lime. The metal ores are placed
in the electroliser and simple manipulation separates
the sulphides. A test on copper ore shows 98 percent
raw copper was able to be gained. Final experiments are
now underway which are expected to be completed within
this year. Installation of the new process will signalize
the disappearance of the huge dirty smokestacks and great
economy of fuels and the appearance of small, simple and
clean smelting factories.(Domei in English).

production of cotton, Manila hemp, copra, tobacco leaf

sufficiency economy of the Co-rosperity Srhere hes been

projeoted. Japan will not begrudge assistance in the way
of capital and technology until the islands attain
complete self-sufficieney, but it rests on the Filipinos
themselves to manage their economy.

PREFACE
The laws and official documents in this collection have
been selected to illustrate Japanese techniques of occupation
in certain of the territories conquered by Japan between 1931
and 1942, and also to serve as a collection of the key laws
affecting the political, social, and economic structures of
those territories during the period of Japanese occupation
or domination.
The territories for which documents are included.are
Manchuria or "Manchoukuo", Inner Mongolia, North China,
Central China, and Thailand. The State Department has
already published a related collection of documents for the
Philippine Islands.
A number of laws and official documents pertaining to
Japan Proper have been included with the object of showing how
the forms of government and administration, and the social,
economic, and financial contróls in occupied areas are made
to conform to those of Japan itself and also of indicating
the manner in which these territories have been and are being
incorporated into the Japanese Empire.

INTRODUCTION.
The administration of the territories occupied by Japan
since 1930 is centered in the Imperial Japanese Cabinet at
Tokyo. Within the Cabinet, three Ministries are concerned
with the formulation and execution of administrative policy,
the Greater East Asia Ministry and the Ministries represent-
ing the Army and Navy. As the armed services have tmposed a
military dictatorship upon the country and are in control of
the territories, they determine colonial policy. In 1942
the Greater Fast Asia Ministry was created by them in order
to centralize the adninistration of civil affairs in a
single agency under Jabinet direction and to relieve officers
engaged in the conduct of military operations of the burdens
of civil administration.
The Cabinet Planning Board, is also concerned with
colonial administration. As its name indicates, it is the 
general planning agency of the Japanese Cabinet. One,of its:
duties is to draft, in accordance with policies established
by the Cabinet, the detailed plans for the administration
of the occupied territories.
: ?
The direct administration of the territories is car-
ried out through a series of local governments, each founded
upon the institutions and traditions of the area and staffed
largely by natives under the supervision of Japanese officials
and advisers. In the formation and use of such governments,
the Japanese are applying a fundamental policy of adminis-
tration common to the totalitarian powers. This policy is
the insulation of the ruling power from direct contact with
the native population by the use of local institutions and
such individuals as can be made or relied upon to serve the
purposes of their conqueror in exchange for political power.
In the former Chinese territories of Manchuria, Inner
Mongolia, North China and Central China, where Japan was
faced with the problem of cutting all ties with free China,
nominally independent governments have been created ostensi-
bly as restorations of older forms of government. Through-
out the conquered territories in the South, the colonial
governments established by the Dutch, British, and Americans
have been taken over and collaborationists and Japanese
citizens placed in control. The government of Thailand,
which capitulated without a struggle, is collaborating with
the Japanese; no important changes have been made in its
organization.

=== Page 266 === (confidence 0.98)
- iii--
: Although the local governments are completely dominated
by the Japanese, their functions are restricted. .In general,
they are permitted to handle domestic affairs, while external
relations among the territories and between each territory
and Japan are reserved exclusively to the Greater East Asia
Ministry.
The social and political control of native affairs in
the territories is also characterized by use of local insti-
tutions and traditions wherever feasible. Thus, the Japanese
have made full use of schools, religious institutions and
local police organizations. They have also.created around
the provincial traditions of the territories a system of
totalitarian parties resembling the parties set up by the
Nazis in occupied Europe.
In Manchoukuo, after resolving the initial problems of
pacification and of economic and political organization;: the
Japanese embarked upon a policy of gradually adopting modern
Japanese institutions. A centralized police system having
the same scope  and functions as its Japanese model has been
set up, while a system of courts has been established and
legal codes adopted which differ little from:their Japanese
counterparts. A similar pattern is being worked out in the
other conquered Chinese territories.
Economically, an attempt is being made:to incorporate
the occupied territories into an antarctic empire system under
direct Japanese contro1. "In the former Chinese provinces,
control of raw máterials,-strategic industriés, communications,
trade, and finance has passed into Japanese hands, and a com-
prehensive development of all resources has been initiated:
In the southern territories, where only the initial'phases of
occupation have been completed, the Japanese have not engaged
in the economic development of: the area, but instead have
followed a policy designed to socure the continued production
of raw materials and certain critidal-supplies upon which
Japan is dependent.
 The'specific economic-techniques employed by the Japanese,
are more involved and deserve a more detailed consideration.
The main features of Japanese tethniques in the field of finance,
industry, trade, and agriculture are described below.
Finance
The policies adopted by the Japanese in this ffeId con-
stitute a technique of finandiai domination which, without

=== Page 267 === (confidence 0.99)
-- 1v -
noteworthy variations, has been applied throughout all con-
quered areas.
Immediately upon occupation, the invading Japanese
Army makes use of a special Japanese currency — the military
note -- for payment of foods and services obtained from the
local population. The military note has no special backing.
By proclamation, it is made legal tender for all.transactions
in territories under the jurisdiction of the Japanese Army.
In its form, denomination and type, the military note tends
to approximate the local currency in circulation prior to
Japanese invasion.
The pre-invasion local currency is maintained in circu-
lation until conditions make it possible to withdraw it in
favor of a new local currency issued by a newly-established
central bank, or in exchange for Japanese military notes de-
nominated in the local currency unit of account. The aim of
Japanese monetary policy in occupied territories is the
issue, by a local central bank, of a local currency attached
to the Japanese yen at a fixed rate of exchange. When this
is achieved, the military yen or notes in local units of
account are withdrawn and exchanged for the new local currency.
In Manchuria, during the years 1931-1935, the Japanese
Army placed in circulation notes issued by the Bank of Chosen.
During the hostilities between the summer of 1937 and the
fall of 1938, the Japanese Army used notes of the Bank of
Chosen in North China and notes of the Bank of Japan in
Central China; military notes were also used to some extent
in both areas. The practice of. using in occupied territories
currency also circulating in Japan had disturbing effects
: upon Japan's monetary structure. This practice was consequently
abandoned in-the autumn of 1938. During all subsequent periods
of occupation, military notes were used exclusively: military
yen notes in China and: Hongkong, military pesos in the
Philippines, military dollars in, Malaya, and military guilders
in the Netherlands Indies.
Between 1938 and 1941 no official exchange rates were
fixed with regard to the military yen in China, although the
Japanese Army Stabilization Fund in Shanghai intervened fre-
quently in 1940 and 1941 with a view to stabilizing the pre-
vailing market rate between the military yen and the Chinese
currency. After the opening of the Pacific War, the Japanese
military authorities enforced a series of official exchange
rates between the military yen and the Chinese. currencies
(the national, yuan issued by the Chungking.Government, the
Central Reserve yuan issued by the Japanese-dominated Nanking

=== Page 268 === (confidence 0.99)
Government, and the Hongkong dollar). Since the military notes
issued in Northeastern Asia were denominated in local units
of account, their issue did not call for the establishment
of a rate of exchange. So far no official exchange rates have
been set between the Japanese yen and these military notes.
Immediately after the establishment of a central govern-
ment in the occupied area, the Japanese authorities proceed
to organize a central bank. This bank usually has a monopoly
of note issue in the area, fulfills the functions of fiscal
agent, conducts general banking business, and has the duty
to supervise and guide the local money market. The capital
of the bank is either provided by the local government alone,
or in conjunction with Japanese and local banks. Where neces-
sary, working credits in the form of renewable six months'
advances are granted to the local central bank by a Japanese
banking syndicate, composed of three official banks -- the
Yokohama Specie Bank, the Industrial Bank of Japan, and the
Bank of Chosen. Control over the local central bank is
vested in the local Ministry of Finance, which in turn acts
in accordance with the monetary and financial policy of the
Japanese Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Japan.
The administration of foreign exchange control, es-
pecially as regards control over foreign trade, is vested
exclusively in a Japanese official bank, the Yokohama Specie
Bank, which acts as the sole agent of the local central
bank and the Bank of Japan in all foreign exchange matters.
The development of local resources proceeds strictly
in accordance with the policies of the Japanese Government.
Capital investments are confined to industries considered
essential by the Japanese and are made through the agency of
special companies owmed or controlled by the Japanese
Government.
Financial control is thus maintained effectively in
Japanese hands. The activities of local banks are de facto,
if not legally, restricted to purely domestic transactions
which have no bearing on the international position of the
local area and its overall economic development.

Trade
In Japan proper control over foreign trade, which is
exercised by the Department of Pinance and the Department of
Commerce and Industry, began with the Exchange Control Law
of 1933 and the Law for the Temporary Control of Imports and
Exports of September 1937. These laws conferred fairly wide
powers which were invoked by ministerial orders only as the
prolongation of the China War and the worsening international
situation dictated. The Exchange Control Law gave the Minister
of Finance authority to regulate all exchange transactions
and transactions in gold and foreign assets. Down to 1936
these powers were exercised with great restraint. There were
no restrictions on foreign trade and no restrictions on the
purchase or sale of foreign exchange for the purpose of im-
porting or exporting commodities. Imports were not controlled
until 1937. War-time control of trade did not actually begin
until September 1937 with passage by tho Diet of the Law for
the Temporary Control of Imports and Exports which was to ex-
pire one year after close of the so-called "China Incident".
This law empowered the government to restrict or prohibit
the import or export of commodities as well as their distribu-
tion and consumption.

Agriculture
Control of agriculture in Japan Proper has been highly
systematised and centralized. The system rests fundamentally
on a widespread network of agricultural cooperative societies,
combined with a government-controlled purchasing organization.
In Manchuria, during the early years of the Japanese
ocoupation, agriculture was to a large extent left to take
care of iteelf. The Japanese were concerned mainly with rail-
way building; foreign markets were open for the soye bean
de, and there was no yen-bloc food deficiency such as de-
later. By 1939-1940 these condi tions had greatly
Peed and fertiliser deficiencies were fording Japan
increesed production of agricultural oreps in

=== Page 274 === (confidence 0.99)
Manchuria. The technique adopted was patterned directly upon
that used successfully in Japan Proper. Early in 19l0 exist-
ing agricultural societies in Manchuria were merged into an
all-embracing Agricultural Development Cooperative Associa-
tion. In July 1941 a single company, the Manchuria Agricul-
tural Produce Corporation, was given exclusive charge of the
purchasing of agricultural commodities.
Regimentation of the farmer has been enforced only
partly through agricultural cooperatives, although these are
being utilized where available and extended as far as pos-
sible. Requisitions are more commonly enforced by direct
compulsion, either through the Japanese military or their
puppet officials in the countryside.
For Southeast Asia, little direct evidence of the tech-
niques applied to the control of agriculture has yet become
available. Except for cotton, the problem in most of the
southern territories is one of dealing with surpluses, notably
in sugar and rubber. Transfer to the cultivation of cotton
is being sedulously fostered, 'in some cases through previously
established cooperative societies, and encouragement is being
given to the growing of foodstuffs in order to achieve local
self-sufficiency.
