I. GOVERNMENT
Introductory Note
The government of Japan is based upon the Gonstitution
granted by the Meiji Emperor in 1839 (infra). There are no
amendments,
The formal provisions of the Constitution provide for
a Constitutional Monarchy. The Emperor is the religious and
temporal ruler of the state (Articles 3 and 4). The execu-
tive functions are exercised by Ministers of State who are
chesen by him and are responsible only to him (Artioles 10
and 55). The Diet consists of a House of Peers, appointed by
the Emperor, and a House of Representatives, elected by bal-
lot as provided in a separate law (Articles 33, 34 and 35).
The judicial system is also organized under a separate law
(Articles 57); however, the courts have no authority to pass
upon the constitutionality of any law.
Under the Constitution, the power of supreme military
command is vested in the Emperor (Article ll ) who exercises
command not through the Departments of War and Navy but
through the chiefs of the General Staffs of the Army and
Navy. In turn, the General Staffs are independent of the
Cabinet and the Diet and discharge their business under the
Emperor's direct control and supervision.
Prior to the granting of the Constitution, Japan had
been a feudal state ruled by a military caste under a sacred
and nominally supreme Emperor. The Constitution did not
destroy this system of government, although it gave it new
form. 1 It declered the Emperor to be the sacred and
supreme ruler, while the executive, which continued to re-
present the ruling class, was made the dominant uranch of the
government by concentrating a preponderance of authority in
the hands of the ministers. Nor was the Diet made a re-
presentative body.
1 "That express provisions concerning the sovereign power
are especially mentioned in the Articles of the Constitution
in no 'way implies that any newly-settled opinion is set forth
by the Constitution; on the contrary, the original netional
polity is by no means changed by it, but is more strengly con-
firmed." Ito, Commentaries on the Constitution of the Empire
of Japan, 2.

=== Page 280 === (confidence 0.98)
-2 -
The House of Peers, whose members were appointed by the
Emperor from the nobility and royelty, was given coordinate
authority with the House of Representatives, and, under the
principles of national polity governing the relation of the
Japanese people to the Emperor, the Diet was intended to be
subservient to the wishes of the Emperor.2
Within this framework of government, the Army and
Navy gained a dominant position in the Cabinet shortly be-
fore the invasion of ilanchuria in 193l. Once in power,
they proceeded to reorgenize the government on totalitarian
lines. Within the Cabinet, control was centrelized by
giving the Premier supervisory authority qver newly establish-
ed government organs, and by combining a number of linistries
in his hands. Other chenges eventually left the Diet without
any real power. Its plarning functions were gradually as-
sumed by the Cabinet Planning Board, created in l937, and all
semblance of independence was destroyed by the dissolution
of the traditional political partics in l94l and the election
of govornment-sponsored candidatos in l942.

The Constitution of the Empire of Japan
February 11, 1889
Having. by virtue of the glories of Our Ancestors, as-
cended the throne of a lineal succession unbroken for ages
eternal; desiring to promote the welfare of, and to give
development to the moral and intellectual faculties of Our
beloved subjects, the very same that have been favoured with
the benevolent care and affectionate vigilance of Our Ancestors;
and hoping to maintain the prosperity of the State, in concert
with Our people and with their support, We hereby promulgate,
in pursuance of Our Imperial Rescript of the 14th day of the
10th month of the l4th year of Meiji, a fundamentel law of State,
to exhibit the principles, by which e are to be guided in Our
conduct, and to point out to whet Our descendants and Our
subjects and their descendants are forever to conform.
The .rights of sovereignty of the State, We have in-
herited from Our Ancestors, and We shall bequeath them to Our
descendants. Neither We nor they shall in futuro fail to wield
them in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution
hereby granted.
We now declare to respect and protect the security of
the rights and of the property of Our people, and to secure to
them the complete enjoyment of the same, within the extent of
the provisions of the present Constitution and of the law.
The Imperial Diet shall first be convoked for the 23rd
year of Meiji, and the time of its opening shall be the date
when the present Constitution comes into force.
When in the future it may become necessary to amend any
of the provisions of the present Constitution, We or Our suc-
cessors shall assume the initiative right, and submit a project
for the same to the Imperial Diet. The Imperial Diet shall
pass its vote upon it, according to the conditions imposed by
the present Constitution, and in no otherwise shall Our des-
cendants or Our subjects be permitted to attempt any alteration
thereof.
Our Ministers of State, on Our behalf, shall be re-
sponsible for the carrying out of the present Constitution, and
Our present and future subjects shall forever assume the duty
of allegiance to the present Constitution.
(His Imperial Majesty's Sign-Manual.)
(Privy Soal.)

session and prorogation of the Imperial Diet, shall be effected
simultaneously for both Houses.
In case the House of Representativos has
been ordered to dissolve, the House of Peers shall at the same
time be prorogued.
Article 45. Then the House of Representatives has been
ordered to dissolve, Members shall be caused by Imperial Order
to be newly elected, and the new House shall be convoked with--
in five months from the day of dissolution.
Article 46. No debate can be opened and no vote can be
taken in either House of the Imperial Diet, unless not less
than one-third of the whole number of the iembers thereof is
present.
Article 47. Votes shall be taken in both Houses by
absolute majority. In the case of a tie vote, the President
shall have the casting vote..

Article 48. The deliberations of both Houses shall be
held in public. The deliberations may, however, upon demand
of the Government or by resolution of the House, be held in
socret sitting.
Article 49. Both Houses of the Imperial Diet may re-
spectivoly present addresses to the Emperor.
Article 50. Both Houses may receive petitions pre-
sented by subjects.
Article 5l. Both Houses may enact, besides what is
provided for in the present Constitution and in the Law of
the Houses, rules necessary for tho managoment of their
internal affairs.
Article 52. No Momber of either House shall be held
responsible outside the respective Houses, for any opinion
uttored or for any vote given in the House. When, however,
a Member himself has given publicity to his opinions by
public speech, by documents in print or in writing, or by
any other similar means, he shall, in the matter, be amenable
to the general law.
Article 53. The Members of both Houses shall, during
the session, be free from arrest, unless with the consent of
the House, except in cases of flagrant delicts, or of offenses
connected with a state of internal commotion or with a foreign
trouble.
Article 54. The Ministers of State and the Delegates
of the Government may, at any time, take seats and speak in
either House.
Chapter IV. The Ministers of State and the Privy Council
Article 55. The respective Ministers of State shall
give their advice to the Emperor, and be responsible for it.
All Laws, Imperial Ordinances and Imperial
Rescripts of whatever kind, that relate to the affairs of the
State, require the countersignature of a Ministor of State.
Article 56. The Privy Councillors shall, in accordance
with the provisions for the organization of the Privy Council,
deliberate upon important matters of State, when they have been
consultod by the Emperor.

Chaptor V. The Judicature
Article 57. The Judicature shall be exercised by the
Courts of Law according to law, in the name of the Emperor.
The organizution of the Courts of Law
shall be determined by law.
Article 58. The judges shall be appointed from among
those, who possess proper qualifications according to law.
No judge shall be deprived of his position,
unless by way of criminal sentence or disciplinary punishment.
Rules for disciplinary punishment shall be
determined by law.
Article 59. Trials and judgments of a court shall be
conducted publicly. When, however, there exists any fear,
thut such publicity may be prejudicial to peace and order,
or to the maintenance of public morality, the public trial
may be suspended by provisions of law or by the decision of
the Court of Law.
Article 60. All matters that fall within the competency
of a special Court, shall be specially provided for by law.
Article 6l. No suit at law, which relates to rights
alleged to have been infringed by the illegal measures of the
administrative authorities, and which shall come within the
competency of the Court of Administrative Litigation specially
established by law, shall be taken cognizance of by a Court
of Law.
Chapter VI. Finance
Article 62. The imposition of a new tax or the mod-
ification of the rates (of an existing one) shall be determined
by law.
However, all such administrative fees or
other revenue having the neture of compensation shall not fall
within the category of the above clause.
The raising of national loans and the con-
tracting of other liabilities to the charge of the National
Treasury, except those that are provided in the Budget, shall
require the consent of the Imperial Diet.

II. MILITARY ORGANIZATION AND DOCTRINE
Introductory Mote
The excerpts from the Inperial Rescript of January 4,
1888 to the soldiers and sailors (infra) give the basic tenets
of the ideology of service to the Emperor, which not only under-
girds morale in the army but underlies the political and social
organization of the country.
The Field Service Code of January 8, 194l (infra) applies,
in a series of precepts, the ideology set out in the Imperial
Rescript of January 4, 1888. The only provisions of the code
dealing with the treatment of the property and persons of non-
combatants are contained in Paragraphs (6) and (7) of Chapter
III. In substance, they contain general prohibitions against
molesting the people or their property. However, the circumstan-
ces under which property may be requisitioned, seized or destroyed
are not defined; such actions are to be taken only " in keep-
ing with regulations under orders from a conmanding officer."

=== Page 318 === (confidence 0.99)
-40 -
Excerpts from "Imperial Rescript To The Soldiers and Sailors"
à
January 4, 1882
Soldiers and sailors, We give you the following precepts:
(1) The soldier and the sailor should consider loyalty
their essential duty. Who that is born in chis land can be want-
ing in the spirit of grateful service to it? No soldier or
sailor, especially, can be considered effecient unless this spirit
be strong within him. A soldier or a sailor in whom this spirit
is not strong, however skilled in art or proficient in science,
is a mere puppet; and a body of soldiers or sailors wanting in
loyalty, however well ordered and disciplined it may be, is in an
emergency no better than a rabble. Remember that, as the protec-
tion of the state and the maintenance of its power depend upon
the strength of its arms, the growth or decline of this strength
must affect the nation's distiny for good or for evil; therefore
neither be led astray by current opinions nor meddle in politics,
but with single heart fulfil your essential cuty of loyalty, and
bear in mind that duty is weightier than a mountein, while death
is lighter than a feather. Never by failing in moral principle
fall into disgrace and bring dishonour upon your name.
(2) The soldier and the sailor should be strict in observ-
ing propriety. Soldiers and sailors arc organized in grades,
from the Marshal and the Admiral of the Fleet down to the private
soldier or ordinary seaman; and even within the same runk and
grade there are differences in seniority of service according to
which juniors should submit to their seniors. Inferiors should
regard the orders of their superiors as is uing directly from Us.
Always pay due respect not only to your superiors but also to
your seniors, even though not serving under them. On the other
hand, superiors should never treat their inferiors with contempt
or arrogancc. Except when official duty r quires them to be
strict and severe, superiors should trcat their inferiors with
consideration, making kindness their chief aim, so that all
grades may unite in their service to the Emperor. If you,
Soldiers and Sailors, neglect to observe propricty, treating your
superiors with disrespect and your inferiors with harshness, and
thus cause harmonious cooperation to be lost, you will not only
be a blight upon the forces but also be unpardonable offenders
against the state.
(3) The soldier and the sailor should esteem valour. Ever
since the encient times valcur has in our country been held in
high esteem, and without it Our subjects would be unworthy of
their name. How then may the soldier and the sailor, whose

=== Page 319 === (confidence 0.99)
-41 -
profession it is to confront the enemy in battle, forget even
for one instant to be valiant? But there is true valour and
false. To be incited by mere impetuority to violnt action can-
not be called  ve valour. The s ldier and the shilor should
have pound di: irimination of right ane wront, cultivate self-
posse: lor, an: iorm their plans with deliberation. Never to
despise un inferior enemy or fear a superior--this is true valour.
Those who thus appreciate true valour should in their daily in-
tercource set gentleness first and aim to win the love and esteem
of others. If you affect valour and act with violence, the world
will in the end detest you and look upon you as wild beasts. of
this you should take heed.
(4) the soldier and the sailor should highly value faith-
fulness and righteousness. Faithfulness and righteousness are
the ordinary duties or man, but the soldier anc the sailor, in
particular, cannot be without them and remain in the ranks even
for a day. Faithfulness implies the keeping of one's word, and
righteousness the fulfilment of one's duty. If then you wish to
be faithful and righteouc in uny thing, you must carefully consi-
der at the outset whether you can accomplish it or not. If you
thoughtlessly agree to do something that is vague in its nature
and bind yourself to unwise obligations, and then try to prove
yoursclf faithful and righteous, you may find yourself in great
streits from which thcre is no escape. In such cases your regrets
will be of no avail. Hence you must first mak, sure whether the
thing is right ous and reasonable or not. If you are convinced
thut you canuot possibly koep your word and maintain righteousness,
you had better abandon your engagement at one. Ever since the
ancient times there have been reptated instances of great men and
heroes who, overwhelmed by misfortune, have perished and left a
tarnished name to posterity, simply because in their effort to be
faithful in sinall matters they failed to discern right and wrong
with reference to fundamental principles, or because, losing
sight of the true path of public duty, they kept faith in private
relations. You should, then, take serious warning by these
examples.
(5) The soldier and the sailor should make simplicity
their aim. If you do not make simplicity your aim, you will be-
come effeminate and frivolous and acquire fondness for luxurious
and extravagant ways; you will finally crow selfish and sordid
and sink to the last degree of baseness, so that neither loyalty
nor valour will avail to save you from the contempt of the world.
It is not too much to say that you will thus fall into a life-long
misfortune. If such an evil once makes its appearance among
soldiers and sailors, it will certainly spread like an epidemic,
and martial spirit and morale will instantly decline. Although,
being greatly concerned on this point, We lately issued the

=== Page 320 === (confidence 0.99)
-42-
Disciplinary Regulations and warned you against this evil, never-
theless, being harassed with anxiety lest it should break out,
We hereby reiterate Our warning. Never do you, Soldiers and
Sailors, make light of this injunction.
These five articles should not be disregarded even for a
moment by soldiers and sailors. Now for putting them into prac-
tice, the all important thing is sincerity. The five articles
are the soul of Our soldiers and seilors, and sincerity is the
soul of these articles, If the heart be not sincere, words and
deeds, however good, are all mere outward show and can avail
nothing. If only the heart be sincere, anything can be accom-
plished. Moreover. these five articles are the Grand Way of
Heaven and Earth and thc universal law of humanity, easy to ob-
serve and to practice. If you, Soldiers and Sailors, in obed•
ience to Our instruction, will observe and practice these prin-
ciples and fulfill your duty of grateful service to the country.
it will be a souroe of joy, not to Ourself alone, but to all
people of Japan.
The 4th day of the lst month of
the 15th Year of Meiji.
(Imporial Sign Manual)

of Japan, Tokyo, pp. 227-229.

Field Service Code Of Japan
Adurten by the War Department on anmary 9, 1041
Introduction
The battlefield is where the Imperial Army, acting under
the Imperiul command displays its true character, conquering
whenever it attacks, winning whenever it engages in combat, in
order to spread Kodo 1/ far and wide so that the enemy may look
in awe to th: cu ust virtues of liis Majesty. Those who march to
the batolefi ld, therefore, should cndeevour to cxelt throughout
the world the glories of the rmpire by fully realizing what the
country stands for and firmly upholding the moral tenets of the
Imperial Army.
The Imp rial Rescript to thc armed forces is explicit,
while the regulations and mrnuals clcerly define the conduct in
combat and methods of training. Conditions in the zone of com-
but, however, tcnd to causc soldicrs to bu swayed by immcdiato
events and become forgetful of their duty. Indeed, they should
be wary th re lest they run counter to their duties as soldiers.
The purpose of this code is to provide conerete rules of conduct,
in the light of past experience, so that those in the zone of
combat may wholly abide by the Imperial Rescript to enhance the
moral virtues of the Imperial Army.
Chapter I.
1. The Empire
Japan is the Kokoku 2/ The Tenno 3/ rules over it ever-
lastingly in a line unbroken through the ages as the successor in
the high and broad cause established by the Imperial Ancestor at
the time of the founding of the Empire. Imperial benevolence is
extended to all without favour, while the Imperial virtues

2. The Imperial Army
The Army, under command of the Emperor, assists in fur-
thering the Imperial fortunes by enhancing the glories of the
Empire through the embodiment of the lofty spirit of valour.
This spirit is the basic factor in realizing universal peace;
for it is the spirit of justice combined with valour and of val-
our tempered by benevolence, in conformity with the Imperial
wishes. Valour requires strictness, while benevolence must be
universal. Should there be an enemy who dares to oppose the
Imperial Army, the Army must resolutely resort to force of arms
and deal him a crushing blow. However, even though force may
compel the enemy to submit, should a lapso in virtue occur by the
striking of those who do not resist or by failure to show kind-
ness to those who surrender, it cannot be said that such an army
is perfect.
Modest in its strength, unostentetious in its kindness,
the Imperial Army becomes the object of admiration when it
quietly displays its valour and benevolence.
The mission of the Impcrial Army lies in making the
Imperial virtues the objects of universal admiration through the
exercise of justice tempered with mercy.
3. Discipline
The essence of discipline in the Imperial Army lies in
the lofty spirit of complcte obedioncc to His Majesty, the Grand
Marshal. High and low must havc deeply engraved in their minds
the solemnity of the right of command; thosc above should exercise
the right in all seriousness, whilc thosc bclow should obey the
the commands in the utmost sincerity. Essential to victory and
requisite for maintaining peace is the condition wherein the
entire Army, united in the bonds of absolute loyalty, moves as
one in response to a command.

Especially on the battlefield is the utmost observance
of the spirit of obedience necessery. The spirit of the soldier
is best exemplified by those who silently do their duty, joy-
fully braving deathin obedience to a command given at a time
when they are undergoing treet hardships.
4. Unity
The Army looks up in awe to His Majesty as its august
head; it must be united in compliance with the Imperial Will,
as one in spirit and in body and in single-hearted loyalty.
In keeping with the basic principles of command, an army
unit should form a solid yet genial group with its commander as
its centre.
It is e ssential that each man, high and low, dutifully
observing his place, should be determined always to sacrifice
himself for the whole, in accordance with the intentions of the
commander, by reposing every confidence in his comrades, and
without giving even the slightest thought to personal interest
and to life or death.
5. Cooperation
Soldiers should not only be united in mind in carrying
out their tasks, but should display the spirit of cooperation
by forgetting themselves for the sake of victory.
Every unit should carry out its mission with responsi-
bility, upholdingits honour, placing confidence in others and
assisting one another, volunteering to face hardships, exerting
all its strength in cooperation and fighting valiantly to achieve
its objective.
6. Aggressiveness
Aggressiveness should constantly prevail in combat, which
must be carried out with bravery and determination. When attack-
ing, be determined and positive, always taking the initiative,
fighting vigorously and stubbornly, vowing not to cease until
the enemy is crushed. In defense, always retain the spirit of
attack and always maintain freedom of action; never give up a
position but rather die. In pursuit, be thorough and inexorable.
Act boldly intent upon victory; be fearless and calm,
meeting the situation courageously, undergoing hardships with
indomitable perserverance so as to overcome all obstaoles.

Fuith is strength. he who hes feith in combat is

The destiny of the Empire rests upon victory or defeat
in battle. Do not givs up under any oircumstances, keeping in

the Imperial Army with its tradition of invincibility.
Chapter II.
1. Piety
The Gods look upon us from above.

Salutes must be strictly executed' in the field. If a

4. The Way of Comrades in Arms
Comrades in arms, united in life and in death for the

5. Initiative in Exemnlary Conduct

Action is prized in the field. Leaders should provide

6. Responsibility
Duty is sacred. One's responsibility is extremely heavy.
Each and every task must be performed with the utmost care, un-
til all available means are exhausted. Those who have a strong

7. View of Life and Death
The lofty spirit of self-sacrificing service to the State
must prevail in life and in death.
Do your duty with heart and soul, regardless of life or
death. After exerting all your powers, spiritually and physic-
ally, calmly face death rejoicing in the hope to live in the
eternal cause for which you serve.
8. Honour
Strong are those who have a keen sense of honour.
Meet the expectations of your family and home community
by making effort upon offort, always mindful of the honour of
your name. If ulive, do not suffer the disgrace of being a

9. Simplicity and Fortitude
Let simplicity guide your daily life on the battlefield,
promote the habit of fortitude and high morale.
Live on the field must be plain; consider privation your
daily lot and endeavour to be thrifty; luxury saps valour.

IV. ORGANIZATION OF HE NATIONAL CONOMY FOR WAR
Introductory Note
In accordance with the Army's plan for total war, laws
have been adopted providing for the mobilization and use of
all resources as part of the war effort.
The basic law on the subject, the National Mobiliza-
tion Law, was originally passed in 1938 and, in an extensive-
ly revised form, was repassed in 194l (infra). The revisions
were all in the direction of greater control over labor, capi-
tel, industry and commodities.
Application of the provisions of the National Mobiliza-
tion Law is through the issuance of Imperial Ordinances, a
long series of which have, been issued, since 1938.
The National.Service Requisition Ordinance (infra) was
1ssued on July 7, 1939 pursuant to the provisions of Article
4 of the National Mobilization Law. Its purpose is to pro-
vide an adequate eupply of workere for the occupations deemed
essential to, netional mobilization.

V. NATIONAL SECURITY
Introductory Note:
The Japanese have dealt with subversive activities
against the state in a series of laws entitled Peace Pre-
servation Laws. The first of these laws was passed in 1925
for the ostensible purpose of curbing communist activity.
Partially revised in 1938 by an Imperial Ordinance, it was
superseded on March 8, 1941 by a more drastic and compre-
hensive law (infra).
The scope of this law appears from the phrase (Nation-
al Polity", which comprehends the political theory of the Jap-
anese state and embodies the peculiar form and concept of the
organic state, the constitution and the relation of the people
to the Imperial line, as showm by sentiments, loyalty, devotion,
and obedience. The law can therefore be applied to any activity
conflicting vith the current trend of "thought control".
The National Defense Security Law (infra) covers secrets
concerning "diplomatic, financial, economic or other important
state affairs, and which are required to be concealed from
foreign countries from considerations of the defensc of the
State". The law is broad cnough to cover all secrets of im-
portance in total war which are not covered by the two laws
relating to military secrets and secrets involving military
resources (infra).

- 87 -

Law For Safeguarding Secrets of Military Material Resources of Japan
Law No. 25 of 1939

Article 1. This law aims at the prevention of leakage
of information to foreign nations concerning matters respect-
ing the manpower and material resources which are to be em-
ployed for military purposes (inclusive, as hereinafter under-
stood, of what is liable to be employed for military purposes),
and for the achievement of national defense.

VI. EDUCATIONAL RELIGIONS AND SOCIAL CONTROLS
Introductory Note
The Imperial Rescript on Education, October 30,
1890, (infra) mirrors the emperor worship ideology of
Japan. Reindoctrination in the ideology was one of the
earliest post-l93l trends inside Japan. General Sadao
Araki, as Inspector General of Military Education, re-
emphasized the Emperor mythos first in the training of
conscripts and later as Minister of Education in the
general school system.
Under the Religious Body Law of Japan, April 8,
1939, (infra) Christian churches in Japan have been
placed under the control of Japanese officials.

VII. ALEIN PROPERTY AND BUSINESS TRAHSACTT ONS
Introductory Note
On July 28, 19l1 1/ , the day following President
Roosevelt's proclamation freezing Japanese assets in the Unit-
ed States, the Japanese government issued an ordinance (inira)
regulating all monetary, financial and property transactions
within its jurisdiction by "nationals of designated coun-
tries". The United States, Great Britain, the Netherlands and
their colonies and possessions were imnediately thereafter
designated as countries subject to the crdinance.
On December 22, 1941, the Enemy Assets Control Law
(infra) was passed authorizing the expropriation in general
terms of all enemy property in Japan. This was followed by an
ordinance (infra) dealing with the administration of the law
and finally by regulations (infra) pertaining to the acquisi-
tion, control and disposition of all assets subject to the law.

VIII. FINANCE
Introductory Note
Banking. Financial institutions, according to Japanese law,
are divided into two categories: special institutions, which
are those chartered by special law and entrusted with objects
and functions of public interest, and ordinary institutions
which are institutions established under general laws with
the object of facilitating the circulati on of capital.
All banking and other Pinancial institutions are under
the supervision of the Ministry of Finance, which, in addi-
tion to its fiscal and treasury operations, exercises direct
administrative functions and conducts financial operations in
the market through the Bank of Japan. The Bank of Japan is a
special institution serving as a central bank. With the
reorganization which took place at the beginning of 1942, a
sunmury of which is given (infra), the bank vwas also made the
contral institution in the industrial fiold and tho inter-
nntional control agency in the monetnry and credit structuro
of the wholo yen area. In its activities in international
finance and industrial inv,stment, tho Bank of Japan doos not
act diroctly but through tho Yokohuma Specie Bank nnd the
Industrinl Bank of Japan. The Bank of Chosen and the Bank of
Taiwan are entrusted with providing logal means of paymont
and ccting as centrrl vanks in coloninl .rons of the Empiro.
Other Japanese spocial bunks include: tho llypothec
Bank of Jnpin which makus long-term loans on mortgagos and
provides funds to coopurativo institutions (mainly through
the Central Bank for Industrial Associations); the Contral
Bank for Commercial nd Manufacturing Associntions which
finances foroign trnde, manufacturing and commercial coopern-
tivo societi es; and tho nowly ostablished Tar Finance Bank
which finences thc uxpansion of producti vo capacity, tho
disposal of idlo or incomplote industrial equipment, and tho
stabilizution of industrial stock firms. Japanese "ordinary"
financial institutions include comnorcial banks, trust
companies, savings banks nnd cooporative crodit societies.
Thore aro six "big" commorcirl banks: tho Dai-ichi, Mitsui,
Mitsubishi and Yasudn with head officcs in Tokyo, and the
Sumitomo nnd Sanwn with hond offices in Osnkn. The various

esteblished and maintained through banking syndicates, clonring
houses, stock oxchenges, and bankers'.associations.

Foreign Exchange Control. Foreign exchange control was first
introduced in Japan in 1932. During the next ten years the
foreign exchange policy passed.through three phases of develop-
ment.
The first phase was characterized by measures designed
to prevent the flight of capital. These measures - similar to
those adopted by other countries in the initial stage of
exchange control - were embodied in the Law for the Prevention
of Flight of Capital, which was enforced beginning July 1,
1932, with the object of controlling purchnses and payments of
exchange, remittances to foreign countries and investments in
securities in foreign currencies.
This phase was short-lived, ending in May l933, when
the Foreign Exchange Control Law was put into operation. The
second phase continued until April 194l. During these eight
years the law underwent partial revisions on four occasions
for the speoific purpose of conserving foreign exchange. In
addition to subjocting all transnctions in foreign exohange
to license by the Foreign Exchange Control Bureau of the
Ministry of Finance, the law gave authority to the government
to require any person to sell to the Bank of Japan gold and
foreign oredits, securities end assets.
As a rosult of the continued prosecution of the Chinese
"Incident" and the deterioration in Japan's relations with
the Unitod States and the British Empire, the older rogulations
were fundamentally revised by tho law of March 194l (infra),
enforced as of April 12, 1941: Since this date foreign exchange
control has becomo less of an economic measure for oonserving
foreign oxchange and more:of a political instrument of agonomic
warfare. The revised law ompowers:the government to control
the methods and conditions of intornntional financial settle-
ments, and to issuo orders pertaining to Japanese property in
foreign countries and to foreign property in :Japan. During
1941, oxchange control played a leading. role in Japan's
economio warfaro in tho Pacific area.
The dotailed rogulations attachod to the law (infra) are
particulnrly important from the administrative point of viow, as
they govern the application and working of foreign exchange
oontrol.
Mhen the United States Governmont issued its so-called
Trossing" ordors in July l94l, -the Japanese Government isaued
an ordinanco'regulating transactions involving the nationals of

exchange transactions with nationals of the designatod coun-

Taxation. Tho first incomo tax law in Japan was passed in
1887. After being amended on several occasions, it was
subjocted to a genernl revision in l940.
The importance of the income tax in Japan's war effort
may bo gauged by the fact that in the budget of 1940-41 it
was oxpocted to provide 46 per cont of tho total ordinary
revenue nnd to cover 19 per cent of the totnl (ordinery and
extraordinary) expendituros.
